title: A great character
hook: and you are of a great character (68:4)

segments.voice: Yesterday: by the pen, the oath that opens al-Qalam. Did you write something by hand? Three verses later, the surah turns from the pen to a person. Day six hundred forty-one.

Mecca, the early years. The Prophet Muhammad ﷺ is being called crazy by people he grew up with, in public, in the market. They say he's lost his mind. Some laugh, some threaten. That's the setting of surah al-Qalam: a man mocked by his own town. Verse two answers the insult: by the grace of your Lord, you are not mad. And then verse four says something nobody in that market would have predicted. It doesn't defend his sanity. It praises his character.

Verse four, in Pickthall's translation: "And lo! thou art of a tremendous nature." Nature is Pickthall's word. The Arabic is khuluq, and most people today translate it character: the moral shape of a person, how they treat others, what they do when nobody's grading them. And the verse says 'azim. Great, immense, tremendous. Khuluq comes from the root kh-l-q, the same root as khalq, creation. Your khalq is how you were made: face, height, voice. Your khuluq is how you've been shaped, the character you carry. One is given. The other, Muslims say, is worked on all your life. Years later someone asked 'A'ishah, the Prophet's wife, what his character was like. Her answer, in Sahih Muslim, is famous: his character was the Qur'an. In other words, if you want to see what the book looks like walking around, look at how he lived. Patient with the people who mocked him. Gentle with children. Mending his own clothes. Another hadith, in the Muwatta of Imam Malik, reports him saying he was sent to perfect good character. And a hadith in Abu Dawud and at-Tirmidhi says nothing will weigh heavier on a believer's scale on the Day of Judgment than good character. It doesn't dismiss prayer or charity. It just says nothing outweighs character. So al-Qalam's answer to the insult isn't an argument. It's a description. You can call a man crazy. But look at how he treats you while you're doing it.

The practice: one good trait, on purpose. Sit, and choose one: patience, gentleness, honesty, generosity, keeping a promise. Just one. Now think of the next place today where it'll be tested. A meeting, a commute, a kid who won't put on shoes, a person who annoys you. Picture yourself there, and picture the trait showing up in one specific action: a softer word, a pause, the truth told plainly. Rehearse it once in your mind, start to finish. The bell holds the time.
Khuluq. Character, the moral shape a person is formed into. In 68:4 the Prophet is praised for a great one: khuluqin 'azim. Today's word.
Your line: great character. Today, practice the trait you picked at least once, on purpose, especially with someone who isn't being kind to you. Day six hundred forty-one.

howItsDone: Muslims treat good character (husn al-khuluq) as central to the faith, and look to the Prophet's conduct, described by 'A'ishah as 'the Qur'an', as its model; many books of hadith have whole chapters on manners and character.

trapdoor: what you thought: the Prophet was a good man.
what it means: the Qur'an answers those who called him mad by praising his khuluq, his character, as great.
what a scholar hears: khuluq and khalq share the root kh-l-q; 'A'ishah's answer, 'his character was the Qur'an', is in Sahih Muslim.
